questions.stem: Coastal sand dunes form mainly through:
options: rivers depositing mud on floodplains during floods
glaciers dropping sediment as they melt and retreat
wind blowing beach sand that plants then trap
waves building rock platforms at the base of cliffs
questions.explanation: Onshore winds blow dry sand off the beach, and pioneer plants such as spinifex trap it, building the foredune. This aeolian process is distinct from wave, river and glacial deposition.

questions.stem: Moving inland from the beach across a dune system in south-east Queensland, vegetation changes from grasses to shrubs and then to woodland. This change is best explained by:
options: rainfall increasing sharply over a distance of a few hundred metres
the soils becoming younger and saltier further from the beach
ecological succession as conditions ease away from the sea
random planting of species by local councils along the coast
questions.explanation: Pioneer plants tolerate salt spray, wind and moving sand. As they stabilise the sand and add organic matter, conditions behind them suit shrubs and later trees, a sequence of succession.

questions.stem: On a meandering river, erosion is greatest on the outside of each bend and deposition occurs on the inside. Why?
options: sediment is carried uphill on the outside and dropped on the inside
water flows fastest on the outside of the bend and slowest on the inside
water flows fastest on the inside of the bend and slowest on the outside
the river is always deeper on the inside, so it erodes the bank there
questions.explanation: Faster, deeper flow on the outer bank undercuts it, forming a river cliff, while slower water on the inner bank drops sediment, forming a point bar. Over time the meander migrates across the floodplain.

questions.stem: The flat land beside a river built up from sediment deposited during floods is called a:
options: tableland
floodplain
headland
foredune
questions.explanation: Floodplains are built from layers of fine sediment left when rivers overflow their banks. Their fertile soils attract farming and settlement, which increases flood risk.

questions.stem: Mangroves grow along sheltered estuaries and bays, such as parts of Moreton Bay. Which conditions favour them?
options: exposed, rocky shores pounded by large ocean waves
cold, freshwater lakes far from any tidal influence
high, dry sand dunes well above the reach of tides
sheltered, muddy intertidal shores in warm climates
questions.explanation: Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees adapted to waterlogged mud in the intertidal zone. They need shelter from strong waves and grow best in tropical and subtropical waters.

questions.stem: Natural grasslands, such as the Mitchell grass downs of inland Queensland, are mainly maintained by:
options: salt spray from the ocean that kills trees across the inland
low, seasonal rainfall with clay soils that crack in the dry season
heavy rainfall all year that allows tall forests to grow quickly
frequent snowfalls that prevent trees from surviving the winter
questions.explanation: Low, unreliable summer rainfall and cracking clay soils favour perennial grasses over trees. These grasslands are widely used for grazing, so stocking rates affect their condition.

questions.stem: Digging channels to remove water from a swamp so that the land can be farmed or built on is called:
options: land drainage
land reclamation
pastoralism
afforestation
questions.explanation: Land drainage lowers the water table and dries out wetlands, a major cause of wetland loss. Reclamation adds fill to create new land, and afforestation is planting trees.

questions.stem: A land use map from 1980 shows a creek valley under forest and grazing; a 2020 map shows most of it as residential estates with a small strip of trees along the creek. The main process of land cover change shown is:
options: pastoralism
land reclamation
glaciation
urbanisation
questions.explanation: The replacement of forest and farmland by housing is urbanisation. Pastoralism is grazing livestock, and reclamation creates new land from water.

questions.stem: Which is a natural process that can change local land cover?
options: a council approving a new shopping centre on farmland
a mining company removing topsoil from a sand island
farmers draining a wetland to plant sugar cane
a cyclone eroding a foredune and its vegetation
questions.explanation: Weather events and hazards such as cyclones, floods and bushfires change land cover naturally, though human activity can increase their effects. The other changes are anthropogenic.

questions.stem: After heavy floods, a riverbank cleared of trees collapses into the river, while a nearby bank with intact riparian vegetation is largely undamaged. This shows that:
options: riparian vegetation has no influence on how banks respond to floods
land cover change is caused by natural processes, never by people
natural and human processes interact to shape land cover change
floods only affect riverbanks that have been planted with native trees
questions.explanation: Clearing (anthropogenic) removed the roots that bind the bank, so the flood (natural) caused far more erosion there. Many local changes result from this interaction.

questions.stem: Sand mining operated for decades on North Stradbroke Island before ending in 2019. Which land cover change did it mainly cause?
options: conversion of mangroves to sugar cane farms along the western shore
growth of new coral reefs on the island's eastern ocean beaches
expansion of rainforest across the island's cleared farmland
removal of vegetation and reshaping of dunes
questions.explanation: Mining removed vegetation and reworked dunes to extract mineral sands, so rehabilitation involves reshaping and replanting. This is an example of resource exploitation as a driver of local change.

questions.stem: On a land use map, a student sees that cane farms reach right to the edge of a creek with no buffer of trees. Which impact on the biophysical environment is most likely?
options: an increase in shade along the creek, lowering water temperatures
more habitat for native birds and animals along the creek banks
more sediment and nutrients entering the creek
less sediment entering the creek because farms hold soil in place
questions.explanation: Without a riparian buffer to trap runoff, sediment, fertiliser and chemicals wash straight into the creek. Removing trees also reduces shade and habitat.

questions.stem: A student overlays aerial photographs of a local wetland from 1990 and 2024 in a GIS and traces the wetland boundary on each. This allows the student to:
options: measure the wetland's water quality in each year
find out who owned the wetland in each year
record the bird calls heard at the wetland
calculate how much wetland was lost, and where
questions.explanation: Digitising boundaries from images of different dates lets GIS calculate change in area and show its location. Water quality and bird surveys need field data.

questions.stem: A wetland covered 48 ha in 1990 and 30 ha in 2024. What percentage of the 1990 wetland was lost?
questions.explanation: The loss is 48 - 30 = 18 ha, and 18 / 48 = 0.375, or 37.5%. 62.5% is the share remaining, and 60% divides the loss by the 2024 area.

questions.stem: Which map type would best show the change in land use across a local catchment between two dates?
options: land use maps of both dates with a common key
a single climate graph for the nearest weather station
a population pyramid for the local government area
a flow map of commuters travelling to the city centre
questions.explanation: Land use maps of each date with the same categories, or a change map derived from them, show where and how land use altered. Climate graphs and population pyramids show other data.

questions.stem: Mangroves along a Moreton Bay shoreline are cleared for a marina. Which implication for people is most likely?
options: lower flood risk, because mangroves block water draining from land
greater erosion and storm surge exposure, and fewer fish nurseries
less coastal erosion because mangroves trap waves and sand offshore
more commercial fish, because mangroves compete with fish for food
questions.explanation: Mangroves dissipate wave energy, trap sediment and provide nursery habitat for many fish and prawns caught commercially and recreationally. Removing them increases erosion and reduces fisheries.

questions.stem: Riparian health refers to:
options: the depth of groundwater beneath farmland in a catchment
the number of houses built within one kilometre of a beach
the condition of vegetation, banks and habitat along a waterway
the amount of rain falling on a catchment in an average year
questions.explanation: Riparian zones are the land along rivers and creeks. Healthy riparian vegetation stabilises banks, filters runoff, shades the water and provides habitat corridors.

questions.stem: Fertiliser runoff from farms and suburbs leads to algal blooms in a creek, which then die and decompose. Which water quality change follows?
options: dissolved oxygen falls, risking fish kills
dissolved oxygen rises, which helps fish
turbidity falls, making the water clearer
pH drops to zero, making the water acid
questions.explanation: Bacteria decomposing dead algae use up dissolved oxygen, a process called eutrophication. Low oxygen can cause fish kills. Algal blooms also make water more turbid, not clearer.

questions.stem: Landfill is a local land management challenge mainly because it:
options: adds nutrients that improve soil fertility nearby
reduces greenhouse gas emissions from household waste
creates new wetlands that need no ongoing management
uses land, and can leak leachate and release methane
questions.explanation: Landfills take up land and, without proper lining and gas capture, can contaminate groundwater with leachate and emit methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Reducing waste extends their life.

questions.stem: Foredunes in front of a beachside suburb have been flattened by foot traffic and the vegetation lost. In a big storm, which outcome is most likely?
options: the storm builds the dunes higher, because bare sand cannot move
erosion is less, because vegetation normally increases wave energy
the beach is unaffected, because dunes play no role in storms
waves erode further inland, threatening property behind the beach
questions.explanation: Vegetated dunes store sand and act as a buffer that absorbs storm waves. Without them, erosion reaches property sooner. Fencing, accessways and replanting help protect dunes.

questions.stem: In the DPSIR framework used to model environmental challenges, the letters stand for:
options: Drainage, Pollution, Salinity, Irrigation, Runoff
Distance, Place, Space, Interconnection, Region
Drivers, Pressures, State, Impacts, Responses
Data, Patterns, Scale, Inquiry, Results
questions.explanation: DPSIR links underlying drivers (such as population growth) to pressures (runoff), the resulting state of the environment (poor water quality), impacts (fish kills) and responses (riparian replanting).

questions.stem: In a DPSIR model of declining water quality in a local creek, 'sediment and nutrient runoff from new housing estates' would be classified as a:
options: pressure
driver
state
response
questions.explanation: Pressures are the direct human activities or emissions affecting the environment. The driver is the underlying cause, such as urban growth; the state is the condition of the creek; responses are management actions.

questions.stem: A student draws a systems diagram showing how dune vegetation, sand supply, wind and storm waves affect each other. The main purpose of such a conceptual model is to:
options: replace the need to collect any data in the field
give exact measurements of sand moved in each storm
prove that only one factor causes dune erosion
show the interconnections behind a challenge
questions.explanation: Conceptual models simplify a system to show how its parts interact, helping explain causes and identify where management could intervene. They complement, not replace, field data.

questions.stem: Which instrument would a student use to measure the cloudiness of creek water in the field?
options: an anemometer
a clinometer
a Stevenson screen
a turbidity tube
questions.explanation: A turbidity tube measures how cloudy water is from suspended sediment or algae. An anemometer measures wind speed and a clinometer measures slope angle.

questions.stem: Students sample macroinvertebrates at three creek sites and find mayfly and caddisfly nymphs at the upstream site but mainly worms and midge larvae downstream of a stormwater drain. This suggests:
options: the upstream site must be polluted because nymphs prefer dirty water
water quality is poorer downstream, as sensitive species are absent
water quality is better downstream, where more worms can survive
macroinvertebrates are not affected by pollution in any way
questions.explanation: Mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies are pollution-sensitive, while worms and midge larvae tolerate poor conditions. Indices such as SIGNAL use these differences to grade stream health.

questions.stem: To measure how vegetation changes from the beach to the back of a dune system, the most suitable fieldwork method is:
options: a single photograph taken from the car park
an online survey of people who visit the beach
a rainfall reading taken once at the beach
a line transect with quadrats at set intervals
questions.explanation: A transect from the beach inland, with quadrats at set intervals, records how plant cover and species change with distance, revealing the pattern of succession.

questions.stem: A student records dissolved oxygen at a creek site at 6 am and again at 3 pm and finds very different readings. What does this suggest about fieldwork design?
options: measurements should be taken at consistent times of day
dissolved oxygen never changes, so the equipment must be faulty
only one reading is ever needed to describe a creek's water quality
readings should be taken at random times so that results vary
questions.explanation: Dissolved oxygen changes during the day as plants photosynthesise and respire. Sampling all sites at similar times, and repeating readings, makes comparisons valid and reliable.

questions.stem: A student wants to test whether riparian vegetation improves water quality. Which fieldwork design is most valid?
options: measure one site with vegetation once and compare it with a textbook value
survey residents' opinions on whether the creek looks healthy
compare a creek in Queensland with a river in another continent
compare matched sites with and without riparian vegetation
questions.explanation: Comparing matched sites on the same creek, sampled at similar times, controls for other variables such as geology and climate, so differences can be linked to vegetation.

questions.stem: Which is primary data for an investigation into dune erosion at a local beach?
options: a council report on coastal erosion published five years ago
Bureau of Meteorology records of storm frequency since 1950
a news article describing damage after a recent storm
dune heights the student measures along a transect
questions.explanation: Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator. Council reports, BoM records and news articles are secondary sources, useful for context and comparison.

questions.stem: Before entering private farmland to sample a creek, a student must:
options: notify the local newspaper
collect samples at night
wear a high-visibility vest only
get the landholder's permission
questions.explanation: Fieldwork ethics and safety require permission to access private land, a risk assessment and respect for the site. Safety gear is part of a risk plan, not a substitute for permission.

questions.stem: Fieldwork shows high turbidity and low riparian cover where a creek runs through a new estate. Which proposed action best addresses the challenge and is most likely to be sustainable?
options: line the creek with concrete so that the banks can no longer erode at all
pipe the creek underground so that it is no longer visible to residents
remove all remaining trees so that sunlight can reach the creek bed
replant riparian vegetation and control sediment on building sites
questions.explanation: Riparian replanting filters runoff and stabilises banks, and sediment fences on building sites address the source. Concrete channels and piping destroy habitat and move problems downstream.

questions.stem: Healthy Land and Water's report card grades the health of waterways in South East Queensland each year. For a student's fieldwork, it is most useful as:
options: primary data that replaces the need for any fieldwork
a land use map showing the location of every house
a climate record showing rainfall since European settlement
secondary data to compare with the student's own data
questions.explanation: Report cards summarise monitoring data collected by others, so they provide context and a check on primary data. They do not replace a student's own field measurements.

questions.stem: When proposing action for a local land or water management challenge, why should a student consider different stakeholders, such as farmers, residents and the council?
options: stakeholder views are opinions and should not influence decisions
actions succeed more often when they balance stakeholders' needs
stakeholders always agree, so their views make no difference
only the council's view matters because it owns all the land
questions.explanation: Sustainable actions balance environmental, social and economic interests. Farmers may support riparian fencing if it is funded and keeps stock out of creeks, for example.

questions.stem: A council plans to protect a beach suburb either by building a rock sea wall or by restoring dunes with fencing and replanting. Which statement best compares the two options?
options: a sea wall always increases the width of the beach in front of it within a few years
dune restoration provides no protection because vegetation has no effect on sand
both options remove all future erosion risk permanently at no ongoing cost
a sea wall shields property but can scour the beach; dunes work with nature
questions.explanation: Hard structures reflect wave energy and can scour the beach in front, while dune restoration keeps a sand buffer that recovers naturally, though it may not suffice in severe storms. Both need maintenance.

questions.stem: Mangroves and saltmarsh capture carbon in their soils at high rates. Protecting them in a local area therefore helps:
options: raise local temperatures by adding dark vegetation to the coastline
increase coastal erosion by trapping sediment in shallow water
reduce biodiversity by shading out other estuary species
mitigate climate change while protecting the coast
questions.explanation: Coastal 'blue carbon' ecosystems store carbon, buffer storm waves and support fisheries, so protecting them has multiple benefits at the local scale.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to present fieldwork findings on how land cover has changed along a creek corridor?
options: a list of every bird species in Queensland, copied from a guide
a photograph of the student's classroom on the day of the excursion
annotated maps of change with graphs of water quality by site
a single paragraph of opinion without any maps, graphs or data
questions.explanation: Maps show the spatial pattern of change and graphs show the measured differences between sites, together supporting evidence-based conclusions and proposed action.
